list.listitem: Aspiration pneumonia is a clinical diagnosis made when a patient at risk for aspiration presents with signs and symptoms consistent with pneumonia. C

Treat suspected aspiration pneumonia as an outpatient with amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin; treat as inpatient with a fluoroquinolone PLUS either clindamycin or metronidazole OR a penicillin/B-lactamase inhibitor. B
Prevention includes strict oral care and, if mechanically ventilated, raising the head of bed and oral antiseptics. B

background.definition: Aspiration pneumonia is an infectious process caused by inhalation of oropharyngeal secretions that are colonized by pathogenic bacteria. It must be differentiated from aspiration pneumonitis, a noninfectious process where inhalation of sterile gastric contents causes lung injury, which may subsequently be complicated by a secondary bacterial infection.

list.listitem: Five percent to 15% of cases of community-acquired pneumonia.
Among 537 adult patients with loss of consciousness from carbon monoxide poisoning, aspiration pneumonia occurred in 19.2%.
Eighteen percent of nursing-home-acquired pneumonia.
Eighteen percent of hospital-acquired pneumonia.

In a study of 47 participating Level I and II trauma centers, the pooled mean ventilator-associated pneumonia rate was 17.2/1000 ventilator days versus 8.1/1000 ventilator days reported by the National Healthcare Safety Network (2006-2008).
Most common cause of death in patients with dysphagia due to neurological disorders.
Among patients with witnessed aspiration in one multicenter cohort study, 16.5% developed acute respiratory distress syndrome.

The development of aspiration pneumonia depends on: (1) risk factors for aspiration events (see Risk Factors section below), (2) aspiration of high-risk contents (more likely with high volume of aspirate, colonization of oropharynx with pathogenic bacteria, or poosr oral hygiene), and (3) impaired host defense (eg, comorbid conditions, decreased immune status, decreased ability to clear aspirate).

Causative organisms include gram-negative enteric pathogens, oral aerobes and anaerobes; species include Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Prevotella, Porphyromonas, Peptostreptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus, Pseudomonas, Serratia, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
There is a trend away from anaerobes in elderly populations.
Chemical pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia are uncommon with tube feedings due to high pH and sterility of the solution.
Aspiration of small amounts of oropharyngeal secretions (microaspiration) occurs in healthy individuals during sleep.
Inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents, often silent and of large-volume (macroaspiration), contaminated with pathogenic bacteria.

Acute pulmonary inflammatory response to acid, bacteria and bacterial products resulting in tissue damage. Inflammatory mediators include chemokines, pro-inflammatory cytokines and neutrophil recruitment.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Endovascular procedure with vs. without intubation (stroke)
Chemoradiotherapy of the head and neck

list.listitem:
Prevention includes oral care with brushing and removal of poorly maintained teeth for elderly patients and those with dysphagia, 24-hour antibiotic therapy for comatose patients following emergency intubation, and use of subglottic secretion drainage and elevating the head of the bed to >30° in mechanically-ventilated patients.
B
Patients with reduced level of consciousness should not be fed orally. C

Other measures that can reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) include proper hand washing, high nurse-to-patient ratio, avoiding unnecessary transfer of ventilated patients, use of noninvasive mechanical ventilation, shorter weaning period, avoiding nasal intubation, preventing bio-film deposition in the endotracheal tube, maintenance of adequate pressure of endotracheal cuffs, avoiding manipulation of ventilator circuits, semi-recumbent position, and adequate enteral feeding. B
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors may reduce dysphagia after stroke and should be considered as the preferred agents for blood pressure control after stroke. B

For patients undergoing elective procedures, the American Society of Anesthesiologists recommend fasting for 2 (clear liquids), 4 (human milk), or 6 hours (light meal, formula) prior to the procedure to minimize aspiration. C They do not recommend routine use of any medication (e.g., gastric acid blockers, antacids) prior to elective procedures for this purpose.
Tube feeding does not reduce risk of aspiration pneumonia in elderly patients.

Remove devices such as feeding tubes and endotracheal tubes when possible. Authors of a Cochrane review found percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) had a lower probability of treatment failure than use of a nasogastric tube feeding, but there were no differences in mortality or complication rates, including aspiration pneumonia (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46-1.06).

Use of metoclopramide was helpful in reducing the rate of aspiration and pneumonia in patients who were within 7 days of stroke onset and 48 hours of insertion of a nasogastric feeding tube in one RCT of 60 patients. There was no mortality difference.

In a retrospective propensity-matched comparison of 2912 pairs of adult patients without cancer requiring nutritional support, patients receiving enteral nutrition compared to parenteral nutrition had lower mortality rates at 30 and 90 days (5.7% vs. 7.6% and 9.9% vs. 12.3%, respectively) despite having higher rates of pneumonia (15.5% vs. 11.9%).
Among patients undergoing PEG placement, there is no difference between early and delayed feeding (>4 hours after placement) on rates of pneumonia or mortality.

Evaluating patients for post-surgical dysphagia should be considered. In one RCT of 438 patients who underwent lung resection surgery, fewer cases of postoperative pneumonia were diagnosed among those randomized to clinical assessment of dysphagia before the initiation of oral intake compared to those receiving usual care (6.4% vs. 12.3%). Dysphagia was diagnosed in 8 of 219 patients (3.7%) of the experimental group.

Prophylactic antibiotics in addition to dysphagia care did not prevent pneumonia in an RCT of 1224 patients with dysphagia after acute stroke (13% developed pneumonia vs. 10% among control patients). Similarly, prophylactic antibiotics did not improve outcomes in children with mild respiratory illness after kerosene ingestion.

Benefit of oral care is uncertain; authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs found mechanical oral cleaning or chlorhexidine reduced pneumonia risk (RR 0.61; 95% CI 0.4-0.91), but , in a second meta-analysis, benefit was only seen for patients undergoing cardiac surgery (RR 0.56; 95% CI, 0.41-0.77) but not for other surgical patients In addition, mortality was increased with use of chlorhexidine in ventilated patients.

In one small RCT in elderly patients, nicergoline (an ergot derivative) was comparable to imidapril (an ACE inhibitor) in improving dysphagia and reducing recurrent aspiration pneumonia over 6 months of treatment.
Use of the chin-down posture only avoided aspiration in 55% of 47 patients with acquired brain injury. Data also support feeding patients who suffered a stroke in a semirecumbent position.
Prophylactic antibiotics (1-2 doses of a ceftriaxone, cefuroxime or ertapenem) appear to reduce the risk of early-onset pneumonia in intubated, comatose patients.
Antimicrobial-coated ETTs have also had beneficial effects on VAP incidence, but cuff shape does not appear to matter.
Authors of a metaanalysis of 13 RCTs in patients on ventilators concluded that the use of subglottic secretion drainage reduced VAP.

In mechanically-ventilated patients , cuff pressure should be maintained at 20 to 25 cm H2O. The role of oral antiseptics in mechanically-ventilated patients and others at risk of aspiration is unclear.
Diagnosis is nonspecific and based on risk factors for aspiration and a pulmonary infiltrate, typically in gravity-dependent areas of the lung. C
Attempt to differentiate from aspiration pneumonitis, which does not require antibiotic treatment; aspiration pneumonitis typically has a more dramatic presentation with hypoxemia and wheezing. C
Oxygen desaturation >2% following 50 mL water swallow, abnormal gag reflex, and abnormal communication suggest aspiration in a patient following stroke. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Often witnessed aspiration, dramatic presentation (hypoxemia, wheezing), improvement without antibiotics
Lack of risk factors for aspiration

list.listitem: Suspect aspiration pneumonia in patients with a history and physical exam consistent with pneumonia in the setting of patient risk factors for aspiration or with proven aspiration events.
Ask caregivers about history of perceived swallowing problems and risk factors for aspiration (see Risk Factors section) or prior aspiration events.

Using videofluoroscopy as the gold standard, use of the ordinal risk rating of the Mann Assessment of Swallowing Ability (a proprietary bedside assessment tool) vs. the total numeric score was better for identifying probable or definite aspiration. The ROC analysis demonstrated an area under the curve of 0.74 (95% CI, 0.66-0.82).

Order speech-language pathologist evaluation for history of swallowing difficulties or risk factors for dysphagia. Patients with dysphagia should have videofluoroscopic swallow evaluation or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) to guide dietary modification. In one Japanese nursing home study, videoendoscopy showing signs of ‘silent aspiration of saliva’ or ‘aspiration of saliva’ was a significant risk factor for pneumonia and a body weight loss of 3% or more.

Physician or speech therapist assessment is only modestly accurate for determining the presence of aspiration in the setting of acute stroke. The most sensitive elements of the assessment are absent gag reflex on the affected side, abnormal involuntary cough (although this is very nonspecific), and abnormal ability to communicate.

Authors of a systematic review of 22 studies evaluated the accuracy of a bedside water swallow test, looking at either airway response or voice change as an abnormal test. Studies of a single sip had high specificity and moderate sensitivity (71% sensitive, 90% specific, LR+ 7.1, LR- 0.7), while studies of consecutive sips to drink 90-100 ml without stopping were highly sensitive and therefore good at ruling out aspiration when normal (91% sensitive, 53% specific, LR+ 2.5, LR- 0.17).
Oxygen desaturation more than 2% following a 50 mL water swallow is a good predictor of aspiration poststroke.

Measuring peak airflow during voluntary cough with an analog or digital meter is a suitable alternative to standard pneumotachograph in identifying aspiration risk among patients with Parkinson’s disease.

CXR may demonstrate infiltrates in gravity-dependent portions of the lung. If supine, infiltrates occur in the superior lower lobe or posterior upper-lobe segments, and if upright, look for infiltrates in the basal lower-lobe segments.

Bacteriology typically consists of oropharyngeal colonizers and includes anaerobes along with more typical organisms such as H. influenzae, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and P. aeruginosa. Sputum cultures are often unreliable because it is difficult to distinguish oral bacterial contamination from pathogenic bacteria.
In one study, the best predictors of VAP were a modified Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (threshold at 6) combined with microbiological data from broncho-alveolar lavage.
Procalcitonin and CRP do not appear to be useful in distinguishing bacterial aspiration pneumonia from aspiration pneumonitis and is not recommended for determining antibiotic use.
An elevated lipid laden alveolar macrophage index (>165) is consistent with aspiration in children (98.6% sensitive, 78% specific, LR+ 4.5, LR− 0.02).
Use preventive strategies in at-risk patients.
Refer patients with swallowing difficulties or risk factors for aspiration and patients following stroke or extubation from mechanical ventilation for an oral-pharyngeal swallow evaluation.
Suspect aspiration pneumonia in patients with a history and physical exam consistent with pneumonia in the setting of risk factors for aspiration or with proven aspiration events.
Obtain a CXR; bronchoscopy is often used to confirm aspiration in VAP.
If the CXR is clear and the illness is mild to moderate, suspect aspiration pneumonitis and observe without antibiotic use.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.

The Gugging Swallowing Screen is a reliable and accurate tool for assessing the risk of aspiration following stroke; sensitivity approaches 100%, but specificity is lower (50%-70%). The results can be used to guide dietary recommendations.

Treat suspected aspiration pneumonia as an outpatient with amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin; treat as inpatient with fluoroquinolone PLUS either clindamycin or metronidazole OR a penicillin/B-lactamase inhibitor (). B
For patients with intractable aspiration, consider surgical intervention. C
See for an overview of drug therapy. In most cases of CAP, a single agent is selected.

Anaerobic coverage is clearly indicated only in patients with a history of loss of consciousness due to alcohol/drug overdose or after seizures in patients with concomitant gingival disease or esophageal motility disorders disorders or in patients with necrotizing pneumonia or lung abscess.
An RCT comparing moxifloxacin with ampicillin/sulbactam (initially IV then orally) found no difference in outcomes.

Another RCT found similar clinical cure rates with ampicillin/sulbactam vs. clindamycin. Patients in the latter group with nosocomial aspiration pneumonia also received a 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin, as did those whose culture and sensitivities warranting aerobic coverage.
Glucocorticoids as adjunctive treatment are not recommended in chemical pneumonitis. Antibiotics are considered as empiric therapy in severe cases.
Evidence does not exist to support transpyloric tube instead of gastric tube feeding to reduce aspiration risk.
Early oral fluids and food following surgery does not increase the risk of aspiration pneumonia, but does increase nausea while decreasing the length of stay.

Tracheoesophageal diversion, a procedure in which the trachea is divided with the proximal end anastomosed to the esophagus and the distal end was brought out to the skin as it is in total laryngectomy, can be used to prevent recurrent aspiration.

In a Japanese case series of 32 patients, surgical closure of the larynx (sacrificing vocal function) prevented aspiration pneumonia, with about half the patients able to ingest food orally alone or in combination with tube feeding. Total laryngectomy was similarly shown in a Texas case series of 23 head and neck cancer survivors with laryngopharyngeal dysfunction to result in a significantly decreased rate of pneumonia and improved quality of life, restoring oral intake in all patients.
One small study on banxia houpu tang, a traditional Chinese medicine, shows that it reduces pneumonia risk in elderly, demented patients.

In a retrospective study using a large Japanese hospital database, rehabilitation begun within 3 days of admission by physical therapists was associated with a reduction in 30-day in-hospital mortality rates in elderly patients with severe aspiration pneumonia (5.1% vs. 7.1% in patients who did not receive early rehabilitation).
Refer those with history of swallowing difficulties or risk factors for aspiration to a speech-language pathologist for an oral-pharyngeal swallow evaluation.

Order video swallow evaluation (VSE) or FEES if dysphagia is noted clinically. Modify diet based on VSE or FEES, and defer oral feedings for those with a decreased level of consciousness. A study in stroke patients found no difference in outcomes for patients with restricted versus unlimited water.
Increase the head of bed to >30° in ventilated patients.
Order strict oral care in elderly and mechanically-ventilated patients, and remove the endotracheal tube as soon as possible.
Insufficient evidence exists for mechanical diets or thickened liquids.
Oral decontamination with antiseptics reduces VAP. Decontamination with oral antibiotics does not reduce VAP. Neither approach influenced mortality.
If good clinical response, 5-7 days; longer if complicated pneumonia.
Depends on bacteriology, host status, and underlying diseases. C

The number of aspiration risk factors is associated with pneumonia recurrence and mortality; in a study of 322 patients hospitalized with pneumonia, recurrence was seen in 13.0% of those with 0-1 risk factors and 54.2% with 4 or more risk factors. Thirty-day mortality was 2.2% with 0-1 aspiration risk factors and 24.1% in those with 4 or more risk factors.
Patients hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia have higher mortality than hospitalized patients with other forms of CAP (29.4% vs. 11.6%).

Stroke patients who develop pneumonia have three times higher mortality. B In addition, stroke patients who developed aspiration pneumonia and had a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale value of 7.44 or greater were at higher risk of needing additional care (discharge to inpatient rehabilitation, skilled nursing facility, or subacute care vs. discharge home).
Tube feeding is of no benefit in demented elderly patients and does not prolong survival or prevent aspiration pneumonia.
There is no randomized controlled trial evidence to support routine use of acid suppressing drugs for women in labor to prevent aspiration if surgery is needed.
Fasting more than 2 hours before pediatric procedures does not appear to be warranted, but more study is needed.
A case-control study found an association between use of acid suppression medications and pneumonia in children with GERD (12% vs. 2% over 4 months, NNH = 10).
In preterm infants, transpyloric feeding is not recommended over gastric tube feeding and may be harmful.

Among hospitalized children with neurologic impairment, a diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia is associated with more complications and more use of hospital resources than a diagnosis of non-aspiration pneumonia.

cell.label: Suspected diagnosis of pneumonia: hypoxemia, fever, cough, purulent sputum, leukocytosis
Suspect aspiration pneumonia: patient at risk for aspiration and/or pulmonary infiltrates in gravity-dependent areas.
(1) Amoxicillin-clavulanate for 7-10 days OR (2) Clindamycin for 7-10 days.
Prevent further aspiration events: refer to speech-language pathologist; if dysphagia, perform video swallow exam or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing and modify diet based on results.

Defer oral feeding in patients with decreased level of consciousness. Encourage strict oral health care in elderly and in intubated patients, and remove devices such as endotracheal tubes and feeding tubes as possible. Elevate head of bed to >30°.
(1) Respiratory fluoroquinolone for 7-10 days OR (2) B-lactamase inhibitor plus a macrolide OR amoxicillin-clavulanate for 7-10 days (ICU treatment: B-lactam plus fluoroquinolone).
Treat as nonaspiration pneumonia (community acquired or health care associated).

feature.caption: Antibiotic Therapy for Aspiration Pneumonia (Typical Duration of Therapy = 10 Days).
feature.feature_body:
Outpatient
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg orally twice a day or 2 g twice daily if the patient has comorbidities (e.g., chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease; diabetes mellitus; alcoholism; malignancies; asplenia; immunosuppressing conditions or drugs) Clindamycin 300 mg orally 4 times a day (add second- or third-generation cephalosporin for aerobic coverage if warranted by culture results)
Inpatient
Levofloxacin 750 mg orally or IV twice a day and either clindamycin (600 mg IV q8h or 300 mg orally 4 times a day) or metronidazole (500 mg q6-8h IV or orally) Ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5-3 g IV q6h Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV q6h Other options: moxifloxacin 400 mg/d (IV or orally), ticarcillin-clavulanate 3.1 g IV q4-6h, imipenem 0.5-1 g IV q6h or meropenem 1g IV q8h Data from Mandell LA, Wunderink RG, Anzueto A, et al. Infectious Diseases Society of America/American Thoracic Society consensus guidelines on the management of community-acquired pneumonia in adults.
